reason: Sufficient supporting sources are available for a high-impact space story with multiple verified claims.
story: In August 2020, an SUV-sized asteroid named 2020 QG zipped past Earth at a blistering 27,600 miles per hour, coming within just 1,830 miles of our planet's surface. It set the record for the closest non-impacting asteroid flyby ever recorded. The most terrifying part? Nobody saw it coming. Because the space rock approached directly from the blinding direction of the Sun, ground-based observatories were completely blind to it. The Zwicky Transient Facility at Palomar Observatory didn't even spot the object until six hours after it had already made its hair-raising pass. Earth's massive gravity field didn't just let it slide by; it violently bent the asteroid's trajectory, turning its path by roughly 45 degrees. If this 10-to-20-foot rock had actually been on a collision course, it wouldn't have caused a global apocalypse, but it would have violently disintegrated into a brilliant atmospheric fireball.
angle: An SUV-sized asteroid sneaked up on Earth from the direction of the Sun and passed just 1,830 miles away, and astronomers didn't even notice until six hours after it had already gone by.

claims.claim: Asteroid 2020 QG passed 1,830 miles above Earth's surface.
It is the closest known non-impacting asteroid flyby recorded.
The asteroid is approximately 10 to 20 feet (3 to 6 meters) in diameter, about the size of an SUV or compact car.
It was discovered by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) at Palomar Observatory.
The asteroid was detected about 6 hours after its closest approach.
The asteroid approached from the direction of the Sun, making it undetectable beforehand.
Earth's gravity bent or turned the asteroid's trajectory by roughly 45 degrees.
The asteroid was traveling at a speed of roughly 27,600 miles per hour (or about 8 miles per second).
If it had hit Earth, it likely would have broken up and become an atmospheric fireball.
Students and researchers including Kunal Deshmukh, Kritti Sharma, Chen-Yen Hsu, and Bryce Bolin helped identify it from ZTF images.
The close approach occurred on August 16, 2020.
ZTF is funded by the National Science Foundation and NASA.

disputed: Exact timing of closest approach varies slightly in hours and time zones across sources (e.g., 04:09 UT vs 12:08 a.m. EDT / Aug 15 vs Aug 16 depending on local conversion), which scripts should handle by stating the date generally or using UTC/EDT specifics directly attributed to NASA logs.
